families.source: UKHSA post-exposure prophylaxis guidance for varicella and shingles
families.topic: significant VZV exposure, susceptibility, antivirals, immunoglobulin and high-risk contact groups
families.page_title: Guidelines on post-exposure prophylaxis (PEP) for varicella or shingles
evidence_points: PEP assessment requires a significant exposure during the infectious period.
PEP is targeted at people at increased risk of severe chickenpox.
High-risk groups include immunosuppressed people, susceptible pregnant women and certain neonates.
Susceptibility assessment may include urgent VZV antibody testing.
Antivirals are recommended as PEP for eligible at-risk groups.
Selected high-risk neonates may also require intravenous varicella immunoglobulin or IVIG.
Timing from first contact is important when selecting prophylaxis.
Exposure to localised shingles differs from exposure to disseminated shingles or chickenpox.
A contact does not need PEP unless exposure, susceptibility and severe-disease risk criteria are all met.
PEP choice requires individual risk-group, timing, contraindication and product-availability assessment.

families.source: UKHSA hepatitis A immunoglobulin post-exposure guidance
families.topic: hepatitis A close-contact assessment, HNIG eligibility, timing, dosage and co-administration with vaccine
evidence_points: Hepatitis A vaccine is the main post-exposure intervention for susceptible close contacts.
HNIG has a limited additional role for eligible close contacts at higher risk.
Eligibility should follow the national hepatitis A public-health management guidance.
Close-contact assessment considers household-type exposure during the infectious period.
HNIG is most effective when given soon after exposure.
Eligible susceptible contacts may receive HNIG up to 14 days after exposure.
Selected contacts at risk of severe disease may be considered later, according to the guidance.
Rapid anti-HAV IgG testing can avoid unnecessary administration when immunity is likely.
Hepatitis A vaccine and HNIG may be given at the same time at different injection sites.
HNIG eligibility depends on susceptibility, age, immune status, liver disease, exposure type and timing.

families.source: UKHSA hepatitis A prevention and public-health control guidance
families.topic: hepatitis A case management, contact tracing, PEP, outbreak control and pre-exposure immunisation
families.page_title: Hepatitis A infection: prevention and control guidance
evidence_points: The guidance supports public-health management of hepatitis A cases and contacts.
Its objectives include reducing secondary transmission and preventing or controlling outbreaks.
Management is informed by the infectious period and the nature of close contact.
Post-exposure prophylaxis may use hepatitis A vaccine with or without HNIG.
Contact assessment should consider susceptibility and risk of severe disease.
Food handling, shared facilities and household-type exposure can be relevant to transmission assessment.
Outbreak control may require coordinated case finding, vaccination and communication.
Pre-exposure immunisation recommendations are included for relevant risk groups.
A positive result or reported exposure alone does not identify every person who requires prophylaxis.
Action requires case timing, contact intensity, immunity, risk factors and current local epidemiology.

families.source: UKHSA hepatitis B immunoglobulin post-exposure guidance
families.topic: HBIG indications, dosage, timing, newborn protection, occupational exposure and vaccine response
evidence_points: HBIG is used with hepatitis B vaccine for selected high-risk post-exposure situations.
Indications include some infants born to mothers with markers of high infectivity.
Indications can include significant percutaneous, mucosal or non-intact-skin exposure to HBsAg-positive material.
Selected recent sexual contacts of infectious people may require HBIG with vaccine.
HBIG should be administered as soon as possible and no later than one week after exposure.
Vaccine should not be delayed while waiting for HBIG.
HBIG and vaccine can be given at the same time but at different anatomical sites.
Age-based HBIG doses are specified for children and adults.
Previously vaccinated people and documented non-responders require different post-exposure pathways.
Use depends on source HBsAg status, exposure type, vaccine history, antibody response and timing.

families.source: UKHSA policy for babies born to hepatitis B infected mothers
families.topic: maternal HBV markers, neonatal vaccine, HBIG, timing and prevention of vertical transmission
families.page_title: Babies of hepatitis B infected mothers (issued August 2008)
evidence_points: Infants born to HBV-infected mothers are at risk of acquiring infection during the perinatal period.
Transmission risk is higher when maternal HBeAg or high HBV DNA indicates greater infectivity.
All babies born to HBsAg-positive mothers should enter the selective neonatal immunisation pathway.
Hepatitis B vaccine should be given as soon as possible after birth.
Additional vaccine doses are scheduled during infancy and at 12 months under the programme.
High-risk infants should receive HBIG in addition to vaccine.
HBIG for high-risk infants should be given as soon as possible and not later than 48 hours after birth.
Low birth weight can be an HBIG indication regardless of some maternal e-marker results.
Vaccine and HBIG substantially reduce but do not eliminate the need for programme follow-up.
Final newborn management depends on maternal markers, viral load, acute infection status, birth weight and timely delivery.
